q: Explain how Random Forest works.
a: It builds many decision trees and combines them. Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample (rows drawn with replacement), and at every split it only considers a random subset of features. For classification it averages the trees' class probabilities and picks the highest; for regression it averages their numbers. The randomness makes the trees different, so their errors partly cancel and the forest has much lower variance than a single tree.

q: Why is Random Forest better than a single decision tree?
a: A single deep tree has low bias but high variance: small changes in data give a very different tree, so it overfits. Averaging many decorrelated trees keeps the low bias and cuts the variance, so the forest generalises better. The trade-off is less interpretability and a bigger, slower model.

q: What's the difference between bagging and Random Forest?
a: Bagging trains each tree on a bootstrap sample using all features at every split. Random Forest adds random feature selection at each split. Without it, a very strong feature would sit at the top of almost every tree and the trees would be highly correlated. Random Forest with max_features=None is exactly bagging.

q: What is out-of-bag (OOB) error and how is it calculated?
a: Each tree leaves out about 37% of the training rows (its out-of-bag rows). For every training row, collect predictions only from the trees that did not train on it, combine them, and compare with the true label. The error rate over all rows is the OOB error. Example: row 5 was left out by trees 1, 2 and 3; they vote default, default, no-default, so the OOB prediction is default. In scikit-learn: oob_score=True, then read oob_score_.

q: Why does each bootstrap sample contain about 63.2% unique rows?
a: The chance a row is not picked in one draw is \(1 - 1/N\). Over \(N\) independent draws it's \((1-1/N)^N\), which approaches \(e^{-1} \approx 0.368\). So about 36.8% of rows are left out and 63.2% appear at least once. For N = 10 it's 34.9%; for N = 100 it's 36.6%.

q: Is OOB error the same as test error?
a: No. It's a good internal estimate of generalisation, close to cross-validation, but it's computed on the training data. After you've used it to choose settings, you still need an untouched test set for an unbiased final number.

q: Can you use OOB scoring when bootstrap=False?
a: No. Without bootstrapping, every tree sees every row, so no row is ever out-of-bag. scikit-learn requires bootstrap=True for oob_score=True.

q: Can OOB replace cross-validation?
a: For quick tuning, often yes: it's free and close to CV. But it can't respect special splitting needs: time order (train on past, test on future), groups (all rows of a customer together) or a specific out-of-time holdout. In those cases use a proper split.

q: Does OOB protect you from data leakage?
a: No. It only guarantees a tree didn't train on that row. If a feature contains future information, or target encoding was computed on all labels before training, the OOB score will be just as inflated as any other score.

q: Can adding more trees make a Random Forest overfit?
a: No. Extra trees only make the average more stable; the score improves and then flattens. Overfitting comes from each tree being too complex (deep trees, tiny leaves) or from noisy or leaky data. Boosting is different: more rounds can overfit.

q: If deep trees overfit, why does Random Forest use deep trees?
a: A deep tree has low bias and high variance. Averaging many decorrelated deep trees removes much of the variance while keeping the low bias. Shallow trees would lower variance too, but at the cost of underfitting, which averaging can't fix.

q: What does max_features do and why is it important?
a: It sets how many randomly chosen features each split may consider. Lower values make trees more different from each other (less correlated) but individually weaker; higher values make trees stronger but more alike. It's the main knob controlling the bias–correlation trade-off. Defaults: "sqrt" for classification and all features for regression in current scikit-learn.

q: min_samples_split vs min_samples_leaf?
a: min_samples_split: a node needs at least this many rows before the tree will even try to split it. min_samples_leaf: every resulting leaf must keep at least this many rows. The leaf setting directly prevents tiny leaves built around one or two unusual rows, so it's usually the more effective smoothing knob.

q: Which hyperparameters would you tune first?
a: max_features and min_samples_leaf (or max_depth), then class_weight if imbalanced, then raise n_estimators until the OOB or validation score stops improving. Random Forest is relatively insensitive to tuning, which is one of its advantages.

q: Training accuracy is 100% but validation is 75%. What do you do?
a: Near-100% training accuracy is normal for a forest of fully grown trees, so judge on OOB or validation. To close the gap: raise min_samples_leaf, limit max_depth, lower max_features, and check for leakage or a train/validation distribution difference.

q: How is feature importance computed and what are its problems?
a: Default (feature_importances_) is mean decrease in impurity: the total Gini reduction from splits on each feature, averaged over trees. It's biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features and is computed on training data, so a random ID can look important. Permutation importance (shuffle a feature on validation data and measure the score drop) is more reliable. SHAP is best for explaining individual predictions.

q: What happens to feature importance with correlated features?
a: Predictions stay fine, but importance is shared between the correlated features in MDI, so each looks less important than the group really is. Permutation importance can show both as unimportant, because when one is shuffled the other still carries the signal. Group them or use SHAP.

q: How does Random Forest handle missing values?
a: Depends on the library. Older scikit-learn needed imputation (median plus a missing-indicator flag). Newer versions (1.4+) can route missing values during splitting. CART-style surrogate splits are the classic theoretical method. In an interview, say you'd impute with a flag unless the library supports NaNs natively.

q: How do you handle categorical features?
a: scikit-learn needs numeric input: one-hot for few categories, ordinal for ordered ones, out-of-fold target encoding for high cardinality (to avoid leakage). One-hot on very high-cardinality columns hurts, because it spreads the signal over many sparse columns that rarely get chosen.

q: Does Random Forest need feature scaling?
a: No. Splits depend only on the order of values (is x below a threshold?), so scaling doesn't change anything.

q: Can a Random Forest regressor extrapolate?
a: No. Each leaf predicts an average of training targets and the forest averages those, so predictions stay inside the range seen in training. For trends beyond the training range, use linear models or add trend features.

q: Why are Random Forest probabilities often poorly calibrated?
a: The probability is an average over trees that rarely all agree, so it gets pulled toward the middle: true 95% cases come out at around 80%. That's under-confidence. If you need real probabilities (pricing, expected loss), calibrate with CalibratedClassifierCV using isotonic or sigmoid (Platt) scaling.

q: How do you handle class imbalance in Random Forest?
a: class_weight="balanced" or "balanced_subsample", a tuned decision threshold instead of 0.5, balanced bootstrap samples (BalancedRandomForest from imbalanced-learn), and evaluation with PR-AUC or recall at fixed precision rather than accuracy.

q: Random Forest vs XGBoost: which would you choose?
a: Random Forest for a fast, robust baseline with little tuning, noisy labels, or when you want easy parallel training. XGBoost/LightGBM when you can tune and want the best accuracy on tabular data, smaller and faster models, and native missing-value handling. RF reduces variance by averaging independent trees; boosting reduces bias by building trees sequentially.

q: What are Extra Trees and how do they differ?
a: Extremely Randomised Trees choose split thresholds at random (then keep the best of those random splits) and by default train on the full dataset without bootstrapping. Even more randomness gives lower variance and faster training, sometimes with slightly higher bias.

q: Why are trees in a Random Forest trained in parallel but boosting trees aren't?
a: Forest trees are independent: each uses its own bootstrap sample and doesn't need the others. Boosting trees are sequential: each new tree fits the errors left by the trees before it. Boosting libraries parallelise within a tree (split search) instead.

q: What is a proximity matrix?
a: For every pair of rows, the share of trees in which both land in the same leaf. It's a similarity learned by the forest, useful for clustering, outlier detection (rows with low proximity to everyone) and imputation.

q: How would you make Random Forest predictions faster in production?
a: Use fewer trees once the score has plateaued, limit max_depth or max_leaf_nodes, keep the model loaded in memory, batch requests, compile the forest (e.g. treelite), or switch to a compact boosted model like LightGBM.
